bill.title: National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2027
bill.latestActionText: Motion to proceed to consideration of measure made in Senate. (CR S4276)
bill.officialSummary: National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2027 This bill sets forth policies and authorities for FY2027 for Department of Defense (DOD) programs, activities, and military construction as well as the national security programs of the Department of Energy (DOE). Among other elements, the bill authorizes the procurement of various items, including aircraft and ships; sets active duty and reserve component personnel strength levels; sets policy regarding various aspects of military health care and military compensation; sets policy regarding DOD acquisitions and acquisition management, including contracting authorities; sets policy for various matters related to DOD interactions with foreign nations, including matters concerning the Middle East, Europe, and the Indo-Pacific; sets policy for various matters related to DOD cyber operations, cyber forces, cybersecurity, and artificial intelligence; requires DOD to review certain materials (including boron carbide, copper foil, and synthetic diamond) to determine actions to maintain access to critical defense industry components and materials, and report to Congress on such matters; authorizes DOD's Office of Strategic Capital to make equity investments in non-federal entities with respect to batteries and critical minerals, materials, and chemicals; authorizes specified military construction projects and extends the authorization of certain projects from previous fiscal years; and authorizes the National Nuclear Security Administration and the Defense Nuclear Facilities Safety Board. For additional information on the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) see In Focus IF10516, Defense Primer: Navigating the NDAA , and In Focus IF10515, Defense Primer: The NDAA Process .

classification.plainSummary: This bill authorizes funding and sets policy for Department of Defense programs, military construction, and Department of Energy national security activities for fiscal year 2027. It covers procurement of military equipment like aircraft and ships, sets personnel levels for active duty and reserve forces, establishes policies for military healthcare and compensation, and addresses cyber operations and artificial intelligence. The bill also authorizes investments in critical materials and minerals for defense manufacturing and approves specific construction projects at military installations.

industries.rationale: The bill directly authorizes procurement of defense equipment, military construction projects, and sets policy for defense contractors and aerospace manufacturers.
The bill authorizes specified military construction projects and extends authorization for projects from previous years.
The bill requires review of critical materials including boron carbide, copper foil, and synthetic diamond, and authorizes investments in critical minerals for defense applications.
The bill sets policy for cyber operations, cybersecurity, and artificial intelligence programs within the Department of Defense.
The bill authorizes Department of Energy national security programs and investments in critical minerals and materials that may affect energy sector supply chains.

plain.whatItDoes: This bill would set out policies and authorities for the 2027 budget year for Department of Defense programs, activities, and military construction as well as the national security programs of the Energy Department.
plain.whoItTouches: People in the military, and their families.
plain.everydayEffect: If it passed, the change would show up in service, and what the military buys. Nothing has changed yet. Most bills never become law.

method.formula: score = Σ_industries ( donorShare(industry) × billWeight(industry) ), where billWeight = classifierConfidence / Σ classifierConfidence. Range 0–1, read as a weighted share of disclosed itemized money.

ordinary.text: They wrote this bill. Sponsoring a bill about your own district's industry is the ordinary case, not the odd one.
Defense & Aerospace is also the top donor sector for 3 other members from MS. That points to the industry being big in the state, not to anything about this member.

disclaimer: This tool places two public records next to each other: who donated to a member of Congress, and what that member legislated on. Any overlap you see is a correlation, not causation. It is not evidence of a quid pro quo, of influence, or of wrongdoing. Legislators routinely receive support from industries in their district for the same reason they legislate on them: those industries are there.
